title: Fewest Steps to Collect Every Key
statement:
A maze is given as a list of equal-length strings grid. Each character is one cell:

  • '@' is where you start (exactly one), '.' is open floor and '#' is a wall.
  • A lowercase letter is a key; the matching uppercase letter is its lock.

The maze uses the first k letters of the alphabet for some 1 ≤ k ≤ 6: each of those keys and each of those locks appears exactly once. One step moves you up, down, left or right into a cell that is not a wall. You pick up a key by stepping on its cell, and you may step onto a lock only if you already hold its key. Keys are never used up.

Return the fewest steps needed to hold every key, or -1 if that is impossible.

examples.why: Lock A blocks the way to b, so first walk 2 steps left for a, then 5 steps right through A to b.
Up 2 for a, back down 2, then through A and up to b in 4. Walking back over cells you have already visited is necessary.
Key a lies behind its own lock.

constraints: grid[i][j] is '@', '.', '#', or a letter among the first k of a–f / A–F
1 ≤ k ≤ 6; each of the k keys and k locks appears exactly once
hints: A plain BFS over cells fails: after grabbing a key you may need to walk back over cells you already visited. What is missing from the BFS state?
The state is (row, column, which keys you hold). With at most 6 keys, the held keys fit in a 6-bit mask, so there are at most 30 × 30 × 64 states.
BFS over those states. Picking up a key sets its bit; a lock is passable only if its bit is set. The first time the mask is full, the step count is the answer.

explain.intuition:
All steps cost 1, so BFS finds shortest paths, but it needs the right notion of "where you are". Standing on the same cell with key a and without it are different situations: one can walk through lock A, the other cannot. So the BFS state is the cell plus the set of keys held. That is why the second example works: returning to the start with key a is a new state, not a revisit.

With at most 6 keys, the set is a bitmask from 0 to 63, so there are at most 30 × 30 × 64 ≈ 58 000 states. Each is visited once, and the first state reached whose mask has every key bit set gives the answer.
steps: Find the start cell and count the keys k; the goal mask is (1 << k) − 1.
Run BFS from (start, mask 0) with a seen[row][col][mask] table.
For each neighbour: skip walls and locks whose key bit is not set. If it is a key, set its bit in the new mask.
If the new mask equals the goal, return the current distance + 1. Otherwise mark it seen and enqueue it.
pitfalls: Marking cells visited without the key mask. The search then refuses to walk back after picking up a key, as in the second example.
Collecting keys greedily, nearest first. In "b...@a....c" taking the nearby a first costs 16, while going to b first costs 14.
Testing for the goal only when a state is dequeued, after it was already counted, or forgetting that the step onto the last key is the final step.

solutions.title: Dijkstra over (key spot, keys held)
solutions.idea: Only the start and the key cells matter as stops. From each stop and key set, a BFS finds the steps to every key not yet held; Dijkstra picks the cheapest order.

solutions.title: BFS over (cell, keys held)
solutions.idea: Add the set of held keys to the BFS state as a bitmask. Same cell with more keys is a new state.

followups: Each key may open its lock only once and then the key is gone. What does the state need now?
There are 20 keys. The state space explodes; how does the stops-only Dijkstra version help, and when does it still fail?
